availableCommands.name: context-gatherer
availableCommands.description: Investigates the codebase to answer a specific question about it. Deeply analyzes existing code by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture and abstraction layers, understanding patterns, and documenting dependencies, returning a thorough, direct written analysis that explains how the relevant code works and points to the specific files and lines involved. Use it to understand code before you change it: before designing or implementing a change to code you don't already fully understand, start with context-gatherer so your edits are grounded in how the code actually works. When a task requires understanding code you don't already know, dispatch context-gatherer to do that exploration before running your own searches or reads. Rules: 1. Provide a clear, specific prompt that includes your intent: a detailed task description of the context you need and what you're trying to accomplish. 2. The subagent explores the codebase and returns an analysis of your query 3. Trust the returned results. You may still inspect additional code yourself when you need context beyond what was returned. 4. Reuse existing context-gatherer output for related follow-up questions; do not re-invoke on the same question with different phrasing. 5. For multiple distinct questions, dispatch several context-gatherers in parallel, each targeting a different aspect of the codebase.

items.name: architecture-design
items.description: Use when designing new systems or significant features, evaluating architectural trade-offs, choosing between structural approaches, or when a task requires understanding system-wide design before writing code

items.name: auto-review-gate
items.description: Use when you have just generated a plan, task definition, or code changes — mandatory review gate that must execute before presenting any deliverable to the user

items.name: brainstorming
items.description: You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation.

items.name: browser-agent
items.description: Use when a task requires interacting with a web browser — testing UI flows, verifying web app behavior, clicking through screens, reading live web content, or automating browser workflows in Google Antigravity

items.name: confidence-check
items.description: Use before implementing a feature or making significant changes to verify you have enough context and understanding to proceed — prevents wasted effort from proceeding with wrong assumptions

items.name: deep-research
items.description: Use when a task requires gathering information from external sources, researching unfamiliar technologies, validating technical approaches, or answering questions that need current web knowledge before implementation

items.name: dependency-management
items.description: Use when adding new dependencies, deciding whether to update packages, running security audits on dependencies, evaluating library alternatives, or encountering outdated or vulnerable packages

items.name: dispatching-parallel-agents
items.description: Use when facing 2+ independent tasks that can be worked on without shared state or sequential dependencies

items.name: executing-plans
items.description: Use when you have a written implementation plan to execute in a separate session with review checkpoints

items.name: finishing-a-development-branch
items.description: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work - guides completion of development work by presenting structured options for merge, PR, or cleanup

items.name: performance-optimization
items.description: Use when code is slow, resource-heavy, or needs optimization — before making any changes, after profiling reveals bottlenecks, or when designing performance-sensitive systems

items.name: receiving-code-review
items.description: Use when receiving code review feedback, before implementing suggestions, especially if feedback seems unclear or technically questionable - requires technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement or blind implementation

items.name: requesting-code-review
items.description: Use when completing tasks, implementing major features, or before merging to verify work meets requirements

items.name: security-review
items.description: Use when reviewing code for vulnerabilities, implementing authentication or authorization, handling user input, storing sensitive data, or before any feature that touches security boundaries goes to production

items.name: subagent-driven-development
items.description: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session

items.name: systematic-debugging
items.description: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes

items.name: test-driven-development

availableCommands.name: general-task-execution
availableCommands.description: General-purpose sub-agent with access to all tools for executing arbitrary tasks

availableCommands.name: context-gatherer
availableCommands.description: Investigates the codebase to answer a specific question about it. Deeply analyzes existing code by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture and abstraction layers, understanding patterns, and documenting dependencies, returning a thorough, direct written analysis that explains how the relevant code works and points to the specific files and lines involved. Use it to understand code before you change it: before designing or implementing a change to code you don't already fully understand, start with context-gatherer so your edits are grounded in how the code actually works. When a task requires understanding code you don't already know, dispatch context-gatherer to do that exploration before running your own searches or reads. Rules: 1. Provide a clear, specific prompt that includes your intent: a detailed task description of the context you need and what you're trying to accomplish. 2. The subagent explores the codebase and returns an analysis of your query 3. Trust the returned results. You may still inspect additional code yourself when you need context beyond what was returned. 4. Reuse existing context-gatherer output for related follow-up questions; do not re-invoke on the same question with different phrasing. 5. For multiple distinct questions, dispatch several context-gatherers in parallel, each targeting a different aspect of the codebase.
